The Quiet Return of the Night Train

Sleeper services are back on European timetables. The economics are considerably less romantic than the marketing.

By Marta Reinhold · 7 August 2026 · 9 min read

For most of the last two decades the night train was treated as a museum piece with a timetable. Operators retired the carriages faster than they could be repainted, and the corridors that once carried sleepers from Paris to Vienna were handed over to freight and to the early-morning commuter rush. Between 2000 and 2019, roughly two-thirds of Europe's scheduled sleeper services disappeared from the books, most of them without ceremony.

Then, sometime around 2021, the obituary stopped being written. Austria's ÖBB, which had quietly bought up rolling stock nobody else wanted, began adding routes rather than cutting them. Others followed — hesitantly, and mostly with borrowed equipment. The Brussels–Berlin service that launched in 2023 was assembled from three different fleets and a great deal of goodwill.

The romance is real, and it is also the least interesting thing about the revival. What changed was not public affection for sleeping compartments; that never went anywhere. What changed was the price of a short-haul flight relative to its political cost, and the willingness of a handful of transport ministries to underwrite the difference for a decade.

The arithmetic under the duvet

A sleeper carriage carries about a third of the passengers a seated carriage carries over the same distance, and it costs roughly twice as much to clean, staff and turn around. The math only works if the trains run full. Operators talk about load factors the way airlines do, and the numbers they need — north of 85 percent, year-round, including February — are numbers most rail services never see.

That is why the new sleepers look the way they do. The six-berth couchette, long treated as an embarrassment, is back precisely because it is dense; the private cabin with the fold-down basin exists to subsidise it. “We are not selling nostalgia,” one ÖBB planner told me, with the weariness of someone who has said it many times. “We are selling a hotel room that moves, and hotel rooms have occupancy targets.”

Track access charges are the other half of the problem, and the half nobody photographs. A night train crossing four countries pays four different infrastructure managers, on four different tariff schedules, for the privilege of moving slowly through the small hours — when the track is also wanted for maintenance. Harmonising those charges has been on the Commission's agenda since 2016. It is still on the agenda.

“The night train is the only mode of transport where the customer's ideal journey is the one they sleep through entirely. That is a marketing problem and an operational gift.”

Rolling stock is the constraint everyone underestimates. New sleeper carriages take four to six years from order to service, and the order books at the two remaining European manufacturers were full before the revival began. Nightjet's newest fleet was ordered in 2018 and did not carry a paying passenger until late 2023 — a lag that spans two elections in most of the countries the trains run through.

Meanwhile the second-hand market has been picked clean. Carriages that sat rusting in sidings outside Zagreb in 2015 were refurbished and running by 2022, and there is no third tranche behind them. Operators who waited are now bidding against each other for equipment that, a decade ago, they were paying scrapyards to take away.

What the subsidy actually buys

None of this makes the revival fragile in the way its critics claim, but it does make it contingent. Every route that launched since 2021 depends on a public contract with an end date, and the contracts were written when energy prices and aviation taxes pointed in a direction they have since stopped pointing. The math only works if the trains run full. When a ministry reviews the line item in 2028, that sentence is the whole argument.

The honest case for the night train is narrower than its advocates make it and stronger than its detractors allow: on a specific set of city pairs between roughly six hundred and eleven hundred kilometres apart, it moves people at a cost per tonne of carbon that no other intervention in the transport budget comes close to matching. Outside that band it is a lovely way to lose money. The trick, for the next five years, is telling the two apart before the timetable is printed.
